test.title: Do plants make offices work better?

paragraphs.text: Office designers have long claimed that plants make workplaces more pleasant, but for many years there was little research to support the idea. Companies that wanted to save money often removed plants first.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: A study in two large offices in Utrecht tested the claim directly. For three months, one floor of each building was filled with plants while an identical floor was left empty. Staff on the green floors completed tasks around 15 per cent faster.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The researchers offer several possible explanations. Workers on the green floors reported feeling more relaxed and said the space felt less crowded. Measurements also showed slightly lower levels of dust, although the difference in air quality was probably too small to affect performance on its own.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Not everyone benefited equally. Employees who had chosen or looked after the plants themselves showed the largest improvements, which suggests that a sense of control over one’s surroundings may matter as much as the plants.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The study has limits. It lasted only three months, and staff knew they were part of an experiment, which may have influenced their behaviour. The authors call for longer studies in a wider range of workplaces.
paragraphs.label: E
